name: Paku Karen
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 12 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Kato, Atsuhiko. 2018. How did Haudricourt reconstruct Proto-Karen tones? Reports of the Keio Institute of Cultural and Linguistic Studies 49: 21-44.
catalog_locator: sect. 3, pp. 37-39 (also sect. 1 n. on voiced stops: 'Karenic languages that preserve voiced stops are four: Geba, Bwe, Paku, and Monebwa', after Shintani 2002, 2003)
catalog_quote: First, in Geba, Bwe, and Paku, where initial voiced consonants have not been devoiced—in other words, in the Karenic languages where tonal splits did not need to occur—the tones originating from Tone *1 are generally higher than those of Tone *2 (for Geba, see Table 11). Second, in Geba, Bwe, and Paku, while Tone *1 has been split, Tone *2 has not been split. [...] there are nine languages where M2’ and H2’ merged with M1 and H1 (i.e., Pao, Padaung, Gekho [1], Gekho [2], Blimaw, Paku, Monebwa, Thalebwa, Sgaw)
sweep_summary: Paku Karen (paku1238, jkp) is not in the catalog. Both works with stress in the title are Glottolog artefacts: the reference pages for Giorgi 2016 (Italian epistemic adverbs, Benjamins, paywalled; Crossref abstract read) and Churng 2007 (American Sign Language topic/focus prosody, UWWPL 26, open PDF downloaded and read) each carry the note 'Paku Karen [jkp] (computerized assignment from \"phases\")' — an automatic title trigger from Luce 1985 'Phases of Pre-Pagan Burma'. Neither concerns Paku or word stress; priority none. The 137-reference Glottolog list for paku1238 in is very likely dominated by the same 'phases' trigger and should be treated as noise. As a by-product the author preprint of Kato 2021 'Typological profile of Karenic languages' (a works still to obtain from our earlier reading) was found open on Kato's Keio homepage and. it gives only a family-level statement (sesquisyllabic words: unstressed minor first syllable, stressed tone-bearing second syllable; 'Karenic languages generally have sesquisyllabic words') and names Paku only for consonants and negation. No Paku-specific stress statement was found.

new_statements.quote: EPK has many disyllabic words that have an atonal first syllable. These are "sesquisyllabic" in Matisoff's (1973: 84ff) terms, in that they are composed of the unstressed first syllable and the stressed second syllable. [...] SK also has many sesquisyllabic words, such as /kәsà/ 'lord, master', /kәshɔ́/ 'elephant', /θәrâ/ 'teacher', /tәkhwá/ 'cousin', /θәwɔ́/ 'village', /pәnà/ 'buffalo', and /lәpɔ́/ 'wave'. Karenic languages generally have sesquisyllabic words.
new_statements.citation: Kato, Atsuhiko (2021). Typological profile of Karenic languages. In Sidwell & Jenny (eds.), The Languages and Linguistics of Mainland Southeast Asia, 337-367. De Gruyter Mouton (author preprint).
new_statements.reading: CAVEAT: this is a family-level (Karenic) statement illustrated with Eastern Pwo and Sgaw Karen, not a first-hand statement about Paku Karen; Paku is only named elsewhere in the chapter (voiced stops, negation). Reading: Karenic words are tone-bearing monosyllables or sesquisyllables whose reduced first syllable is unstressed and whose final full syllable is stressed — i.e. prominence is on the full (tone-bearing) syllable, no contrastive positional word stress. No Paku-specific stress statement exists in any source opened in this or our earlier reading.

new_statements.quote: D'après les tableaux de Luce, et leur résumé par Jones, la catégorie V est confondue avec la VI en pwo, en blimaw, en Gèba, et même en palaychi ; dans cette dernière langue il y a effectivement un traitement différent de cette catégorie selon que l'initiale est aspirée ou non-aspirée, mais sans rapport avec la distinction V/VI (d'ailleurs Jones doit noter : V, Va, VI, VIa pour cette raison). La distinction V/VI se trouve dans les langues pa-o, kayah, geko, yinbaw, paku et sgaw. La catégorie V ne représente pas dans les langues actuelles (sauf peut-être en yinbaw) un tonème indépendant, mais la série de mots qui ont un ton VI en pwo, et un ton II en sgaw.
new_statements.translation: According to Luce's tables and Jones's summary of them, category V is merged with VI in Pwo, Blimaw, Geba and even Palaychi; in the latter language there is indeed a different treatment of this category depending on whether the initial is aspirated or unaspirated, but unrelated to the V/VI distinction (Jones has to write V, Va, VI, VIa for this reason). The V/VI distinction is found in Pa-O, Kayah, Geko, Yinbaw, Paku and Sgaw. Category V does not represent an independent toneme in the modern languages (except perhaps in Yinbaw), but the series of words that have tone VI in Pwo and tone II in Sgaw.

new_statements.quote: In Sgaw and Palaychi the merger of the two series of initials is incomplete: the *voiced nasals have merged with the *aspirate nasals, but *voiced stops did not become aspirate; they are only voiceless. In the resulting system there is a restriction of co occurrence between initials and tones: the three tones which Burling calls *1, *3, ana [and] *2+ do not occur with aspirate initials. This was to be expected since they derive from the low allotones conditioned by a proto *voiced initial.

sources.quote: EPK has atonal syllables, which are phonetically unstressed and short, and cannot occur utterance-finally. [...] EPK has many disyllabic words that have an atonal first syllable. These are "sesquisyllabic" in Matisoff's (1973: 84ff) terms, in that they are composed of the unstressed first syllable and the stressed second syllable. [...] Karenic languages generally have sesquisyllabic words. [...] In PK and SK, the minor syllable in a sesquisyllabic word never has a tone; however, in some other Karenic languages, it may bear tones.
sources.locator: Preprint sect. 18.2.2 Suprasegmental phonemes, preprint p. 7 (extracted text page 7); Paku named on preprint p. 6
sources.note: Family-level only: Karenic words are monosyllabic or sesquisyllabic, with the minor (first) syllable unstressed and the full second syllable stressed and tone-bearing; examples are Eastern Pwo and Sgaw Karen, with Kayah Li and Kayan cited. Paku itself is named only for retaining Proto-Karen voiced stops with a four-way stop contrast (after Shintani 2003b) and for its verb-negation pattern; there is no Paku-specific stress statement. Read as a tone-language profile with stress = full-syllable vs. minor-syllable, not a positional word-stress rule.
sources.venue: The Languages and Linguistics of Mainland Southeast Asia

sources.citation: ISO 639-3 Registration Authority. 2011. Change Request 2011-059 (split kpp into jkp Paku Karen and jkm Mobwa Karen) with New Code Request forms for jkp and jkm. Dallas: SIL.
sources.note: Nothing. Sociolinguistic/identification only (names Pagu/Paku/Monebwa/Mopha etc., c. 5,300 speakers, 'Paku and Mobwa dialects have not been documented much'); cites Shintani 2003 and Bradley 1997 and an unpublished 2008 SIL survey.

sources.citation: Manson, Ken. 2011. The subgrouping of Karen. Paper and handouts presented at SEALS 21, Kasetsart University, Bangkok (jseals.org/seals21, via the Internet Archive).
sources.note: Comparative-historical (rhyme and initial correspondences, tone boxes); Paku data columns from Luce and survey wordlists; Paku placed in Southern Karen with Sgaw. No statement on stress.

sources.citation: Kato, Atsuhiko. 2008. Geba-go kiso shiryo [Basic materials in Geba]. Asian and African Languages and Linguistics 3: 169-219 (already held by the project under geba1237).
sources.note: About Geba, not Paku; p. 173 reports that Shintani (2003) treated 16 Karenic languages and that only Geba, Bwe, Paku and Monebwa preserve Proto-Karen voiced stops - confirms Shintani 2003 contains Paku phonological data. Nothing on Paku stress.
